summary: Eugène Burnouf worked in Indology, Buddhist studies, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. A pupil of Antoine-Léonard Chézy (c. 1822–1832), he served at the Court of Appeal of Paris (1824) and taught at the Collège de France (1832–1852).

Eugène Denis specialized in Buddhist studies and Indology, earning a Ph.D. from the University of Paris by 1976. He served at the CNRS (1961–1986), became a professor at Chulalongkorn University in 1976, and held a post at Bangkok University.

Eugène Henri Guillaume Edgard Monseur was an Indologist and linguist who studied under Charles Michel at the University of Liège (doctorate, 1884). He served as professor of Sanskrit and comparative grammar at the Université libre de Bruxelles from 1888 to 1912.

Eugène Jacquet specialized in Indology, linguistics, and Sinology. He attended Lycée Louis-le-Grand and studied under Antoine-Léonard Chézy, Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat, Pierre-Amédée Jaubert, Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy, and Eugène Burnouf.

Eugène Obermiller worked in Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and Indology. He studied at Saint Petersburg State University under Theodore Stcherbatsky and later with Dondub Buddhayin, holding posts at the Institute of Buddhist Culture, the Institute of Oriental Studies, and University of Chicago.
Eugène Pittard worked in history and archaeology. He studied at the University of Geneva from around 1887 to 1899 and later held a post there from around 1916 to 1949.

Eugène Tisserant worked in history, archaeology, and religious studies. He studied at Lycee Notre-Dame Saint-Sigisbert, the Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales (c. 1904–1907), and the École du Louvre (c. 1904–1908).

Eugène-Armand Hauvette-Besnault was an Indologist who studied at the Petit Séminaire de Saint-Nicolas-du-Chardonnet and under Eugène Burnouf. He held posts at the École Normale Supérieure, the Sorbonne (1868), and the École Pratique des Hautes Études.
Eugénie Bazin-Foucher worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. She studied at the Sorbonne and at the École Pratique des Hautes Études under Sylvain Lévi from 1915 to 1918.

Eugénie Sellers was a scholar in history and archaeology. She studied at Girton College, Cambridge (1879–1882) and the British School at Athens (1890–1891), later holding posts at Chatsworth House (1904–1908) and the British School at Rome (1909–1925).

Eun Hino is a Buddhist studies scholar who completed a master's course at the University of Tokyo (c. 2004–2006). Hino held appointments at the University of Tokyo (c. 2011–2015) and Musashino University (assistant professor c. 2015–2019, associate professor c. 2019).
Keiun Maeda (1857–1930) was a scholar in Buddhist studies. He served as president of Toyo University and as president of Ryukoku University.

Eun-su Cho is a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy. She earned a PhD at the University of California, Berkeley under Padmanabh S. Jaini, served as assistant professor at the University of Michigan until 2004, and joined Seoul National University in 2004.
Eunyoung Choe is a scholar of Buddhist studies who earned a doctorate from Korea University and served as an HK Professor at Geumgang University (attested 2013–2015).

Eustaquio Echauri Martínez was an Indologist and linguist who studied at the Conciliar Seminary of Pamplona and Universidad Central. He was professor of Latin at the University of Barcelona (1920) and professor of Greek and Sanskrit at Complutense University of Madrid (1940).
Eva De Clercq is an Indologist who earned her PhD from Ghent University between 1999 and 2003, later holding a position there as a permanent member in 2025.

Eva K. Neumaier works in Buddhist studies and Tibetology. As of 2006, she was Numata Professor of Buddhist Studies at the University of Calgary and professor emeritus and former department chair at the University of Alberta.
Eva K. Neumaier-Dargyay is a scholar in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. She studied under traditional teacher Khenpo Rigzin and held a post at the University of Calgary (attested 1992).

Eva Tichy is a linguist and Indologist. She studied under Karl Hoffmann at the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg (Dr. phil. c. 1974–1981), habilitated at the University of Marburg, and held the Indo-European linguistics chair at the University of Freiburg (1993–2017).

Eva Wilden is an Indologist who completed her MA, Promotion, and Habilitation at the University of Hamburg between 1985 and 2004. She was maître de conférences at the EFEO in 2003 and became professor at the University of Hamburg in 2017.
